sweep_summary: Six title hits, all Glottolog. Four are the 1985 ANLC volume and its two Leer chapters (already held as the ERIC ED398761 scan, now copied into the paci1278 folder and re-read): Leer 1985a 'Prosody in Alutiiq' remains the deciding source and its quoted passages are verified in the text (locator note: the 'several possible configurations' sentence is the last lines of p.107, cited as p.108); Leer 1985b 'Toward a Metrical Interpretation' refines the analysis (three stress degrees, unaccented feet reinterpreted as superfoot-adjoined syllables, optional final destressing) without changing placement. The two unlisted items are both ANLA archival items and both turned out to be online: Leer's 1999 manuscript 'Rules for lengthening, stress, and foot formation.. Port Graham and Nanwalek' (downloaded, scanned, checked against the page scan) states in plain terms that stress falls at the end of the foot, heavy CVV syllables are feet by themselves, two light syllables form a foot, initial CVC is a foot, and schwa is never stressed - confirming the catalog's weight coding; the Kosbruk 1983 item is a 40-minute elicitation tape of the example words from Leer's paper (tape notes downloaded, audio left online), primary data rather than a statement. Nothing found supersedes Leer 1985a; the 1999 manuscript is a good open, first-hand corroborating citation.

new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive iambic system: feet are built left to right; a heavy (CVV) syllable is a foot by itself and a pair of light syllables forms an iamb; a word-initial closed light syllable (CVC) forms a foot alone; stress falls on the last syllable of each foot; schwa syllables are never stressed; leftover light syllables attach to the preceding foot. This is exactly the system the catalog codes as 'weight' from Leer 1985a, restated by the same author fourteen years later for the Kenai Peninsula Chugach dialect. It is a 7-page teaching summary without the full argumentation, dialect coverage (Koniag, Prince William Sound) or the final-destressing statement of Leer 1985a, so it corroborates rather than replaces the deciding source.

new_statements.quote: Impressionistic accounts of Chugach Alutiiq prosody describe a uniquely complex metrical system which builds both binary and ternary feet, is weight-sensitive, and demarcates metrical structure via stress, additional lengthening on ternary foot heads, foot-initial onset fortition, and metrically conditioned tone. [...] the ternary distinction between unstressed short, stressed short, and obligatorily stressed long vowels is expressed via all three acoustic correlates. [...] Based on these results, we suggest a revised phonological analysis of Alutiiq as a non-prototypical stress language which associates an H* accent with each stressed syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's weight-sensitive iambic reading (Leer 1985a; Leer 1999 existing statement): the abstract confirms a weight-sensitive foot-based system in which long (heavy) vowels are obligatorily stressed and both binary and ternary feet exist. It adds instrumental confirmation (2,235 vowels, 2,720 onsets, seven narratives) that stressed vs unstressed and long vs short are cued by duration, intensity and f0, and it revises the tonal component of Leer's description (H* on each stressed syllable instead of categorical metrical tones). It does not contradict the placement rule. Only the abstract was read, so this is a corroboration at low resolution, not a replacement of the dec…
new_statements.rule_in_words: At abstract level only: Chugach Alutiiq is a weight-sensitive metrical (foot-based) stress language building binary and ternary feet; long vowels are obligatorily stressed (i.e. a heavy CVV syllable is always a foot head), short vowels may be stressed or unstressed depending on foot position; stress is realised by duration, intensity and f0, and the authors reanalyse the language as a non-prototypical stress language with an H* pitch accent on every stressed syllable rather than a system with independent metrically conditioned tones. No sentence about the direction of footing (iambic, left-to-right), initial CVC feet or schwa was visible in the abstract; those details are in the full text, which could not be opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in the abstract. The abstract implies multiple stressed syllables per word (each foot has a stressed head; 'additional lengthening on ternary foot heads' marks maximal-foot heads), i.e. a rhythmic multi-stress system rather than a single primary stress, but no primary/secondary distinction is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Abstract reports that compression (length neutralisation) was 'not a fully length-neutralizing phenomenon', that additional lengthening on ternary foot heads was expressed by f0 rather than duration, and that the 'so-called tones were not categorically distinguished by f0 as previously described'. These are revisions of the phonetic realisation described by Leer, not of stress placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Alden & Arnhold 2026 describes Chugach Alutiiq (the Chugach dialect of Pacific Gulf Yupik/Alutiiq, Prince William Sound and Kenai Peninsula), the same dialect Leer 1999 describes for Port Graham and Nanwalek; the abstract does not say which villages the seven narratives come from. The catalog's Alutiiq entry rests on Leer 1985a, which also covers the Koniag dialect.

sources.note: weight-sensitive foot-based accent: light = one vowel, heavy = two full vowels; feet defined left to right; heavy syllable = accented foot by itself; two light syllables = iamb with the second accented; word-initial closed light syllable = accented foot on its own (FD-rule IC); stress falls on the accented (foot-final or only) syllable; word-final accented syllables optionally destressed. Verified again in the text we hold layer at every cited page; one locator correction: the 'several possible configurations' sentence sits at the foot of p.107, not p.108.

sources.note: A short, first-hand, community-oriented restatement by the same fieldworker for the Kenai Peninsula (Port Graham / Nanwalek) Chugach dialect: stress is foot-final; feet are a single heavy (CVV) syllable or two light syllables; word-initial CVC forms a foot alone; after the initial foot, three light syllables give L[LL] unless the third has schwa (schwa is never stressed), otherwise pairs of light syllables form iambs; stray syllables adjoin to the preceding foot as a superfoot; stressed foot-final vowels lengthen. Identical weight criteria and left-to-right iambic footing to the coded system.

tone.summary: First acoustic study of Alutiiq metrical prosody: unstressed short, stressed short and obligatorily stressed long vowels are separated by duration, intensity and f0, foot-initial onsets are fortified, compression does not fully neutralize length, and the reported metrical tones are not categorically distinguished by f0. It keeps the weight-sensitive stress system of the catalog entry (Leer 1985) a

sources.quote: In Yupik (Eskimo-Aleut), vocalic overlength in Central Siberian Yupik and the laryngeal “fortition” of consonants in Central Alaskan Yupik (allophonic) and Alutiiq (phonologised; cf. the description in Section 4.1) also show a synergistic alignment within the strong template (the “stressed” foot”), as opposed to the weak template (the “unstressed foot”), but in a different form (see the detailed account in SM2). Lengthening of short vowels and overlengthening of long vowels under stress in open syllables has strengthened the foot nucleus – the stressed vowel, while consonantal fortition – the left boundary of the foot. [...] Leer (1985: 83–87) describes fortis consonants in Alutiiq (Eskimo-Aleut) through a complex bundle of features: as voiceless, tense, longer in duration than lenis (but shorter than geminates), truncating the preceding vowel, pre-occluded, with a preceding hiatus, a reduction of air pressure, or with a schwa-like transition.

sources.quote: Like all other Yupik dialects, Chugach Alutiiq (henceforth Chugach) has iambic rhythm. Leer (1985) reports that in words consisting of light syllables only, stress falls on every syllable in position 3n-1 (i.e. σ2, σ5, etc.), as well as on the final syllable of any words of length 3n+1 (i.e. four, seven) syllables. Lefthand foot edges are detectable by their initial consonant, which is realised fortis [...] Leer marks no primary–secondary stress distinction, and we will follow his transcription here. [operator signs in '3n-1'/'3n+1' read from the parenthetical examples; the text extraction rendered them as 'k'/'j']

sources.quote: Syllables containing a single vowel are called light syllables; those containing two full vowels, heavy syllables; those lacking a final consonant, open; and those having a final consonant, closed. (p. 82) ... phonetic length has become largely redundant, being predictable by prosodic accentuation, closure, and position of the syllable in the word. This is the reason for choosing the terms "light" and "heavy" rather than "short" and "long" to denote whether a syllable has one or two vowels. (p. 88) ... the accented foot (indicated in the prosodic marking by an acute accent over the last (or only) vowel of the foot) and the unaccented foot. The latter is always monosyllabic and except in PWS CA, may contain only one vowel. Accented feet may be monosyllabic or disyllabic, but the number of vowels in the foot is limited to two. (p. 79) ... 1. Unaccented light foot ... Consists of a single light unaccented syllable; produced by FD-rules IIA, IIB, and [IIC] ... 3. Accented light foot ... Consists of a single light closed accented syllable; produced by FD-rules [IC] and IIIB1. 4. Accented heavy foot ... Consists of a single heavy accented syllable; produced by FD-rules [IIIA] and post-FD
sources.locator: Leer, 'Prosody in Alutiiq (The Koniag and Chugach dialects of Alaskan Yupik)', printed pp. 77-133; Deciding passages: sec. 1.2 Syllable structure p. 82; sec. 0…
sources.note: Every element of the catalog 'heavy' text is stated in the work: heavy = two full vowels (p. 82); a single-vowel syllable is light open or closed (p. 82); the word-initial light closed syllable is defined as an accented foot by FD-rule IC (p. 110), the only place a CVC counts for accent by itself; phonetic length is derived from accent (PA-rule 3 p. 88: accented open non-final vowel long, closed or final short; 'compression' of vowel pairs in closed/final syllables p. 89), hence 'light/heavy' not 'short/long' (p. 88). Also confirmed: tone_cls no-tone -- no lexical tone; pitch is assigned by ru

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1985b. Toward a Metrical Interpretation of Yupik Prosody. In Michael E. Krauss (ed.), Yupik Eskimo Prosodic Systems: Descriptive and Comparative Studies (ANLC Research Papers 7), 159-172. Fairbanks: ANLC. [Glottolog 681297]
sources.quote: [p.163] First, it has become increasingly apparent that, unlike the rest of Yupik, Alutiiq has three degrees of stress: zero stress, weak stress, and strong stress. ... [p.164] Thus, those which until now I have been calling "unaccented feet" in Alutiiq are here reinterpreted as syllables joined to the "accented feet" to their left. ... [p.165] In Alutiiq, such destressing is optional ... [p.166] B. Superfoot formation rule: Form a left-headed superfoot on each foot plus any unassigned (light) syllables immediately following the foot. ... [p.168] 4.2. Chugach Alutiiq ... 3. Three syllable rule. Working from left to right, operating on non-initial sequences of three light syllables (S1S2S3) ... (a) define S2S3 as an iambic foot unless S3 is voiceless.
sources.locator: sec. 4 'Alutiiq' p.163 (p.168); p.165 (p.170); sec. 4.1 KA rules pp.165-167 (pp.170-172, rule B superfoot p.166); sec. 4.2 'Chugach Alutiiq' p.168 (p.173)
sources.note: Restates the Alutiiq system of Leer 1985a in metrical terms: feet are iambs (two light syllables, second stressed) or single heavy syllables built left to right; the former 'unaccented feet' are stray light syllables adjoined to the preceding foot in a left-headed superfoot; Alutiiq has three stress degrees (zero/weak/strong); word-final destressing is optional; CA differs from KA by the three-syllable rule and voiceless-syllable avoidance; word-initial CVC forms a foot (rule A1 as in 1985a). Same placement facts as the deciding source; a reanalysis, not new data.
